speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-66, to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act (grant of certificate).

maintopic: ELIZABETH R. CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT PROVISION FOR GRANTING OF CERTIFICATES IN SPECIAL CASES
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: ELIZABETH R. CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP ACT PROVISION FOR GRANTING OF CERTIFICATES IN SPECIAL CASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill I propose to introduce is entitled "An act to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act (grant of certificate)". The purpose of the bill is this. In the Canadian citizenship courts today there are many wives of Canadian citizens who are not granted their citizenship papers because they do not know enough of the English or French language. This is because some of these wives who live in isolated areas and places, and even in urban areas, are not able to assimilate enough of the English or French language to learn sufficient to enable them to receive their citizenship certificates. This bill is to provide that in special cases where a wife has been in Canada for 10 or 15 years but is still not sufficiently
knowledgeable in the English or French language-and there are cases where the children of such a person have become citizens of this country along with her husband-she may be granted a certificate of citizenship.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Shefford inquired concerning the 25 cents per hundredweight supplementary payment made on milk. At this time I should like to clarify the reply I made then.
Under the dairy support program in effect in 1962-63 a supplementary payment of 25 cents per hundredweight was made on all milk used for manufacturing purposes other than that from producers participating in the fluid milk market. For the current support year this 25 cents per hundredweight payment has been increased to 30 cents per hundredweight for milk from eligible shippers whose milk is used for the production of cheddar cheese. This action was taken to provide a modest incentive to the diversion of milk to cheddar cheese production, since both domestic requirement and export opportunities have increased for this product.
For milk used for the production of butter and skim milk powder the 25 cents supplementary payment has been replaced by a purchase program on skim milk powder designed to compensate producers of milk used for this purpose. At the same time the 25 cents supplementary payment was withdrawn on manufactured milk products for which production can be adjusted to meet domestic requirements. This action was based on the premise that such products should not require federal subsidization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the widespread anxiety created by published statements that the greater part of the radioactive debris from the December, 1962 Russian atomic tests, including strontium 90, cesium 137 and carbon 14, is now starting to drift down over Canada, and in view of the fact that such published reports indicate that such debris will settle more heavily on Canada than on any other country in the world, can the minister outline to the house


the steps being taken by the government to protect Canadian livestock and food supplies from the dangers of contamination with its resultant danger to the health of the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MEASURES TO COUNTERACT RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question this morning. While I feel that the steps the government is taking to protect Canadian livestock and food supplies are not properly matters which should be given on orders of the day-and if my hon. friend wishes I shall be pleased to answer a question on the order paper-the matter is of such concern to many Canadians that I should like to comment at least in this way. We are testing air, precipitation, soil, milk, wheat and human tissue. We are bringing samples to Ottawa and having these tested, and we will continue to do so in an intensified way.
However, it is not correct to say that at the moment there are significant quantities of cesium 137. If there is no further atmospheric testing the level is one which, while we are watching it, is not of great concern; that is, it is not dangerous. The levels of strontium 90 and cesium 137 result from the heavy atomic testing of last fall. At the moment it is considered by the department that the levels reached will not be high enough to warrant government intervention, but a very close watch is being kept on this and a plan is prepared for use if necessary.
I should like to assure the hon. member and all hon. members of the house, and through them the country, that the closest attention is being paid to this particular problem.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Justice, and is as follows. In the light of the fact that the almost daily increases in the price of sugar are threatening to put small bakers out of business, can the minister do anything to expedite the investigation which he has already told this house his department is making, in answering questions from the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather)?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REQUEST TO EXPEDITE INQUIRY INTO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have already been two questions on this matter, and perhaps more; one from the hon. member for New Westminster, one from the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), and the hon. member who has just spoken, who sent me notice of his question a few minutes before the house met. I do have a reply on this subject. It is somewhat lengthier than usual but I hope the house will bear with me, because I think this is a matter of some importance.
I should like to put on the record the following information, which was given to me by the director of investigation and re-

search under the Combines Investigation Act. On the morning of May 21, 1963 the refinery price for sugar in Montreal was $16.19 net per 100 lbs. in a paper bag. On May 21, 1962 the comparable price was $7.03. The increase is $9.16. On May 15, 1962 the world spot price for raw sugar was $2.68 U.S., and on May 20, 1963 it was $12.30 U.S. The difference is $9.62 U.S., and when allowance is made for the fact that it ordinarily takes 107 lbs. of raw sugar to make 100 lbs. of refined sugar, the Canadian refiners, who must buy their raw sugar under pricing conditions that are directly affected by world market prices, have had a cost increase of $11.11 Canadian per 100 lbs. of refined sugar.
Between April 8 and May 20, 1963, the world spot price for raw sugar went up by $4.47 U.S. or approximately $4.83 Canadian. In the same period the net refinery price in Montreal increased from $11.98 to $16.19, or by $4.21.
Both these illustrations indicate that Canadian refinery prices have gone up less than the price for raw sugar. The figures given, however, are not completely reliable because they do not show the actual prices at which the refiners, who are continually making purchases of raw sugar for future requirements, have bought, but they are the best available figures for purposes of comparison and do show why the refiners have had to increase their prices. They also indicate that the price advances have not been out of line with increased costs for the basic and essential raw materials.
The two main reasons for lower prices on refined sugar in the United States at the present time are, first, that there is now no tariff on importation of raw sugar into the United States and, second, the United States prices are apparently lower than Canadian prices because of the different exchange values of the United States and Canadian dollars.
The increase in raw sugar prices is said to flow from increased demand, poor beet sugar crops in Europe for the past two years, and poor cane crops in Cuba. Speculation in the world sugar market may also play a part. None of these matters is under the control of the Canadian refiners.
Beet sugar production in Canada is substantial, but it only accounts for about one fifth of the country's requirements. In the present situation, sugar beet growers and beet sugar makers are not in a position to affect the price of sugar in cane sugar consuming areas in any significant way.
It is the practice of the combines branch to scrutinize all notable commodity price movements for the purpose of determining
Inquiries of the Ministry whether there may be cause for inquiry under the Combines Investigation Act. In the case of sugar, the director indicates that price changes of the nature experienced can take place without their necessarily having any significance under that act. The director will continue to keep the matter under surveillance.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 22, consideration of the motion of Miss Pauline Jewett for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to the speech from the throne delivered by His Excellency the Administrator at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to continue from where I left off at six o'clock yesterday, I would like to say to all hon. members, and particularly to all whose mother tongue is French, how pleased I am with the contents of the speech from the throne, and especially paragraphs 6 and 7. I am convinced that without the strengthening of our traditional bonds, and at the same time the recognition of the stimulating contribution of other cultures, this nation cannot flourish as it should. Indeed, it is in danger of disintegration if such steps are not taken. The leadership of the Conservative party never did pay proper attention in this direction, and it is doubtful whether there is still any awakening or realization there. That is the main reason they are back in opposition after such a short parole.
The Prime Minister is to be heartily congratulated, not only for the speed with which he has written to the premiers of the provinces enclosing to each of them the terms of reference for the proposed royal commission of inquiry on bilingualism and biculturalism, but especially for the incorporation in the terms of reference of the expressed provision that:
-the contribution made by the other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada and the measures that should be taken to safeguard that contribution-
-shall be taken into account.
The Prime Minister and his ministers are to be congratulated upon the whole content of the speech from the throne. They have not attempted to crowd the complete Liberal platform into it, as this would have meant biting off more than could properly be chewed. Instead, to the chagrin of the Leader of the Opposition, and contrary to his inclinations, a concise, clear course of action has been charted. It is a course that bespeaks decision and beneficial results for the nation. First things have been put first, and there is a new atmosphere of confidence throughout

Canada as a result of the April 8 verdict of the people and as a result of the insight and drive that the Prime Minister has continued to demonstrate since that day.
My constituents in Spadina will be particularly interested in the measures designed to promote steady employment, the system oi contributory portable pensions, the special assistance for technical training, the changes that will be made in the citizenship act to ensure full equality of rights for all Canadian citizens wherever they were born, and the promised review of immigration policy. The unspecified amendments to the National Housing Act are also of considerable interest.
With respect to employment plans I suggest that wherever possible the work to be done should be taken to the workers or provided in their close vicinity, and not vice versa. In this way the chance of a better future is offered to many persons without their being forced to leave their own environment and seek residence elsewhere, which almost always entails the heartache of separation and difficult periods of adjustment and social integration. This is particularly applicable to the landed immigrant, who should have the benefit of the advice and close association of his friends of his own nationality.
I much appreciate finding in the speech from the throne the paragraph on the establishment of a comprehensive system of contributory portable pensions. I should expect that this would take some time to evolve, due to the complexities of any such proposed system. The new Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and her departmental assistants are to be complimented upon the hard work they have done and must no doubt still do in this respect. I receive many calls about this measure, particularly from the elderly who need and are looking forward to the extra $10 per month.
There are already two provincial institutions in Spadina that have been established for retraining purposes and they are heavily subsidized with federal grants, but more assistance in this direction is needed and particularly in this area to which so many people who lack job security seem to gravitate. The increased technical training of our youth is also a necessity and a priority. In both these connections planning should be so tied in that tradesmen will be trained for as much indoor work as possible in the winter months and as much outdoor work as possible in the milder months, and work when feasible should be scheduled accordingly. This should be given emphasis because of the particular severity of our winters. Our

planning, of course, should be for our country and its problems, and should not blindly follow that of other countries.
It is very pleasing to me that naturalized Canadian citizens will no longer be subject to deportation to their country of origin for catalogued misdemeanours or otherwise, and that they will in future, therefore, be deemed to be equal before our law. This will open the way to discussions with the United States for an agreement whereby our naturalized citizens will no longer be subject to the quota for their country of origin when seeking entry there.
It will, I know, take some time to review the Immigration Act and the regulations now in force under that act, but I am sure this will not prevent this new reform minded Liberal government from humanizing the application of the present harsh and inhuman regulations. Such action is needed and is in accordance with the spirit and tradition of this party. We on this side have always had a warm heart toward the immigrant. We have consistently realized the value to our country and its economy of a much larger population. Our domestic consumers' market still remains far too small to absorb the products of our farms and factories. Under the present circumstances, surely the need to relax regulations respecting close relatives can be met, particularly in respect of brothers and sisters, children over 21 and formally adopted children and their families. Many an immigrant saves sufficient money to sponsor a brother and can provide employment for him, only to be frustrated by the strict letter of some other regulation. The red tape and delay experienced during the last government's tenure of office by applicants for the entry of priority relatives, such as wives, parents and children under 21, should also be cut.
I congratulate the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau) upon his appointment. I remind him that he has power under the act to admit in special cases. I am sure that particularly because he is a Liberal it will not be necessary to remind him to exercise this power generously.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that when it comes to arms for our defence forces we should have the best available that we can reasonably afford to answer known threats, as history proves that only those able and willing to defend themselves survive. I believe that when it comes to co-operation with NATO and NORAD we should do our best to cooperate, for in unity only is there strength. I believe that when it comes to disarmament talks we should, with proper safeguards seek
The Address-Mr. Starr vigorously for an agreement to disarm. I am convinced that when it comes to communism an eye should be kept on the increased activity in central Toronto, as it appears to be leaving its soap boxes and following more respectable means of infiltration.
Both Canada and the United States, Mr. Speaker, are currently countries where 50 per cent of the people have 20 per cent of the wealth and 20 per cent of the people have 50 per cent of the wealth. In the light of this fact I believe that when it comes to questions of planning, and automation versus employment, a new sense of social justice must imbue both our industry and our government, even a good Liberal government which this one so brightly promises to be.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the latter remarks of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) regarding immigration cases I am inclined to revive all my immigration cases and place them again before the new minister in the hope that now they will be disposed of favourably and quickly.
May I first of all, Mr. Speaker, congratulate you on your nomination to the honourable position which you now hold. In my opinion it was a wonderful choice, and every member of the House of Commons is agreed upon it. I am sure that all members of the house will wish you well and that you will apply to your new duties those principles of fairness and impartiality which have been traditional with those in your position.
I should also like to take the opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Lamoureux) on his appointment as Deputy Speaker. I know his task will not be easy in presiding over the committees of the whole house, but I am sure he too will discharge his duties with fairness and impartiality.
I should also like to join those who have preceded me in this debate in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, both of whom discharged their tasks in a worthy manner, particularly the lady from Northumberland, a neighbouring constituency to my own.
So far as the present government are concerned, Mr. Speaker, they can be assured of a high degree of co-operation from the official opposition, that is co-operation in all measures that take into account the realities of the situation and are designed to apply practical solutions to the problems. This I feel we have a right to expect, and this I feel the people of Canada also have a right to expect. The

The Address-Mr. Starr present Prime Minister has a difficult task, but he can be assured that we in the Conservative party will respect the position he holds, something that has been lacking in the past five years. When the Grits were in the opposition, and particularly during the last parliament, they disregarded and degraded the position of the prime minister, and continued to do so in the election campaign which followed. We will respect, Mr. Speaker, and understand the enormous responsibilities which rest upon the Prime Minister's shoulders. We will not allow ourselves, for merely partisan considerations or reasons, to forget that as Prime Minister of Canada he is entitled to consideration and respect from all sides of the house.
I just want to point out to the right hon. gentleman that, after all, he has not a mandate from all the people of Canada. He has a mandate from only 43 per cent of the people of this country, even though he had the advantage of the support of all the newspapers and other media in the metropolitan centres of this country. In spite of this he was only able to achieve a minority government when 43 per cent of the people voted for him. I think he should keep this in mind as he conducts the affairs of this country.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a critical time for Canada. In this critical time all of us, all the members of this house, are called upon to play a responsible and constructive part in the conduct of the affairs of this country. It is a time for enormous and far reaching decisions. I must say that a mere change of government does not alter the deep-cutting issues with which this country is faced. The issues remain, and they must be met.
However, I want to point out that Canada has been faced with problems ever since confederation, and will be faced with problems continuously from this day forward. Any young country which is growing has problems, and those problems must be faced and solutions must be found for them. Solutions must be provided in order that the initiative and energy of industry and labour in this country may continue to serve the economy, and above all that Canadians themselves may benefit to the maximum extent from the products of our labour and the exploitation of the resources of this country. This is a task of government now as it always has been, regardless of what government was in office.
These problems, Mr. Speaker, cannot be solved by presenting them in pious platitudes, nor can the government talk its way around them. I am referring particularly to these highfalutin' platitudes about decisions in 60


days. Decisions are called for now, and action, but that action must be courageous and resolute; because the greatest and perhaps the fatal mistake any government can make at this time is to resort to high sounding phrases which would have a reassuring effect and lull everyone, including the government, into a state of false complacency without coming to grips with the problems. I am afraid this is what is happening at this period of our life in this country. We might be lulled into a sense of security by the thought that we now have a government that has promised to make decisions within 60 days.
The government of which I had the honour to be a member under the leadership of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) addressed itself, regardless of the criticism we have faced, in a positive and practical manner to the tasks as they presented themselves to us. The measures we implemented have brought an unprecedented increase in the economic growth and a record rise in exports, a drop in imports, and a general, across the board increase in employment in this country. During the election campaign there were those who wanted to get the economy rolling, as they said in their propaganda. I say we got it moving, Mr. Speaker, and it is up to the government now to keep it moving.
We have heard a great deal from this government about 60 days of action. Some of the newspapers in the metropolitan areas picked this up and publicized it. As a matter of fact, after this government took office some of the newspapers kept track of the situation from day to day. I know one newspaper in the Toronto area that went so far as the 14th day, on which they publicized an announcement by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) to the effect that there would be 10,000 scholarships available. To this day nothing more has been heard about that, and this newspaper dropped the tabulation on the 14th day because no other action was forthcoming and no decision was made.
As a matter of fact, I believe some of the most important decisions were made in the choice of some of the cabinet ministers who were selected by the Prime Minister. This situation recalls the 100 days of Roosevelt's first term. He did not talk about 100 days of action, he implemented the action during the 100 days and then talked about it. In this country we have the situation reversed. They talk about 60 days of action but no action at all has been forthcoming. I commend this example of Roosevelt's 100 days of action to hon. gentlemen opposite.

The Address-Mr. Starr
As a member of the previous government I had some intimate concern with the problem of unemployment. To the new Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) I express my congratulations and my assurance that he can count upon me for complete understanding of the problems with which he will be faced. During the past several years we heard a great deal from hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in the official opposition, about the problems which beset this country. As I pointed out earlier, Mr. Speaker, a young, growing nation such as Canada will always be faced with problems. Those problems must be resolved in the best way possible by whoever has that responsibility at the time. There has been some reference in this debate to unemployment. I do not wish to go into this subject at the moment to any great extent. The Prime Minister in his speech averaged out unemployment over the years prior to 1957. He also averaged out unemployment during the years since then, and pointed up the great differences that occurred in those years.
During the election campaign hon. gentlemen opposite promised the people of this country full employment. We will give them a reasonable time to implement this promise; then we will assess the results to ascertain whether they meant what they said or whether it was only a hoax perpetrated upon the Canadian people. I remember some of these hon. gentlemen, and I see some of their faces now-the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), who is not here-who showed a great deal of concern over the unemployment problem and certainly brought it to our attention with great vehemence. They were worried about unemployment in the provinces; they were worried about unemployment in their municipalities. It will be interesting to see what these gentlemen who now occupy the treasury benches and have the responsibility and opportunity are going to do about those problems in their provinces and constituencies. We will keep track of what is happening, what the situation is and what the results are.
By the measures implemented in the past two years by the former government we were able to reduce unemployment month by month and increase employment month by month and year by year. It will be interesting to see whether this government with its policies, will be able to continue that trend of decreasing unemployment. If they are not able to increase or at least continue that trend they will certainly hear from us, and I think we will be right in pointing out the serious problem to them. I hope they will
continue to maintain their concern now they are in office. But more important, I hope they will do something about the situation and continue what we started in the past, the results of which are now evident month by month and year by year.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, they will not take the attitude, for example, that because the Prime Minister has taken two trips out of the country, all our international and domestic problems will be solved. After all, we still have not felt the effects of trips which will no doubt be taken by the new Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). I have watched him for a few days, and he has a faraway look. I think he visualizes some of the trips he might be making outside this country. I would say to him if he were here -and he can read it in Hansard-that the most important thing he has to remember is that primarily he is the member for Essex East including the city of Windsor. He was so concerned, and rightly so, about the economic situation in Windsor that he must apply himself to rectifying the situation in that city; then he can make trips abroad.

One of the basic things this country needs, and which it has needed for some time, is vocational training. We dealt with that matter very effectively when we were in office. Because of the tremendous advance made in vocational training we will

have on the labour market skilled and trained young people possessing the basic qualifications which are required for jobs in industry. This is what we did in the short space of two and a half years. I think it is incumbent upon this government to see to it that when these young people emerge from vocational training, jobs will be available for them. We will make sure that we point this out to them from time to time. That is why it is urgent that the machinery of co-operation between management and labour, which we set up through such bodies as the productivity council, be not allowed to lapse into rust and disuse. We need more jobs in Canada. The best way of providing these jobs is through the co-operation of labour and management. They have a very important part to play. Therefore I hope the government will do everything they possibly can to bring about a greater degree of labour-management co-operation in this country.
Another problem is the effect of automation upon the labour force of this country, which is a terribly fearful thing to the older worker. We presented a bill designed to deal with this problem in a specific way. That bill was acclaimed by all who understood it and were interested in it. We hope that the new Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the government will again bring this bill in for consideration by this parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer for a few moments to our school building program designed to give Canadians the advantage of learning new trades and skills. I feel this is one of the basic problems confronting this country. I do not intend to go into detail regarding the expenditure which has been incurred in building these schools. I want to point out, nevertheless, that it is now giving 135,000 Canadians an opportunity to learn new trades and skills. I hope that after a careful assessment of this program, which is ending in October of this year, the present government will come to the proper decision and, if necessary, build more schools in order to provide education of this type for the people of Canada. There is no mention of this in the speech from the throne, even though it represents, in my opinion, the basic solution to the problem of unemployment.
The municipal winter works program has been effective in curbing the steady onset of seasonal unemployment, and I trust the new Minister of Labour will look sympathetically at these arrangements even though the minister of external affairs may be against them; I recall that he dismissed the program as a bagatelle when it was introduced into this house. My own feeling is that it has done well in providing jobs for Canadians each winter on a temporary basis.

I have mentioned labour-management cooperation because I believe this is a field in which the maximum degree of effort is required at the present time. It is a field where such efforts will yield the greatest possible results, because management has a direct and positive interest in increasing the rate of industrial growth while the labour unions have a direct and personal interest in keeping up the supply of new jobs. This is a task which any government must set itself in moving to correct those built-in disabilities which have helped to introduce unemployment. Government can only accomplish this task by enlisting the support of labour and management in a direct and positive way. I must point out that there is a great deal of good will on both sides, good will which must be placed at the service of the economy and of the people of Canada in general.
At this time I should like to say to the new Minister of Labour that he is indeed fortunate in the calibre of those people he will find at his disposal in the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission, people who have been, are, and, I am sure, will be ready and willing to carry forward the policies he may be initiating.
I have mentioned these matters at some length because I believe they are the real problems and issues which must be kept in mind when we examine the outline of government policy as it appears in the speech from the throne. It is not my intention to pull this document apart, sentence by sentence and word by word. However, there are some general remarks which I feel called upon to make at this time. While giving the government the benefit of the doubt, as we are all inclined to do, nevertheless I am forced to point out that there is very little for labour in the speech from the throne. Some of the promises which have been made by the present occupants of the treasury benches, including the Prime Minister, come to mind. I think of the measure to introduce a minimum wage of $1.25, the regulation of hours of work and a number of other things. I have scanned the speech from the throne thoroughly and have yet to find anything in it directed toward labour in this country. There is one sentence relating to automation and manpower adjustment, but it is not clear what that sentence really means. I would think it refers to a bill similar to the one we introduced in the last parliament, and setting out the same policy that was contained in that measure-one, by the way, which failed to pass.
What about the proposal to set up a new department of industry? Will the new minister be able to give direction to industry?
The Address-Mr. Chretien Is that what is intended? If so, where does direction stop and regimentation begin? We should like to hear about this when the legislation setting up the new department is introduced. If the department is not going to give direction, what will be its function? We shall all be awaiting with interest the answers to these questions.
Also to be found in the speech is mention of an economic council to develop more employment and encourage efficient production. I venture to say that if this council is set up no effects will be felt in this country for at least four or five years. In fact there is nothing in this speech from the throne which would have an immediate effect. This economic council appears to be nothing more than a wrapping up of the national economic development board which we proposed and which was held up by the last parliament along with the measure to establish a productivity council. Hon. gentlemen opposite have thrown these into one basket and come up with this idea of forming an economic council.
I have no objection to this, because the measures we introduced were good measures which would have resulted in a continuation of the economic development already under way as a result of the other programs we implemented. But to try to pass these measures off as part of the bold, imaginative Liberal government program is just a little too much to swallow. I think hon. members opposite have perpetrated a hoax on the Canadian people.
They say they are going to set up a municipal loan board. What funds do they propose to make available to that board for loans? Is it $400 million? How much work is that going to provide? The municipal winter works program has seen $900 million spent in five years, giving jobs every winter to 135,000 Canadians for a period of 45 days. Yet hon. members opposite talk about solving the unemployment problem with $400 million. How is this money to be distributed? What criteria will be applied in granting loans to some municipalities and refusing them to others? Can any municipality get them? Is there to be a limit, or will Toronto and Montreal or some other large municipalities get all the money, leaving nothing for the others?

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to represent the riding of St. Maurice-Lafleche, which was set up in 1935, and which, even at that time, through the foresight of its electors, enabled a Liberal government to take over from a Conservative administration. In 1963, the electors of my riding of St. Maurice-Lafleche decided once again to help the Liberal party stop the spread of Social Credit and sound the beginning of the end for that party in the province of Quebec, and also to put in power a Liberal government to replace, once more, a Conservative administration.
Mr. Speaker, I succeed a Liberal member, Mr. J. A. Richard, who sat here for many years and served his riding and the house well. Therefore, on behalf of the electors of the riding of St. Maurice-Lafleche, I wish to pay tribute to that man who, although well in years, represented with dignity for many years the riding that did me the honour to elect me.
Mr. Speaker, since I have been elected, many of my English speaking colleagues have asked me questions on a problem of the day and wanted to know what I thought of the separatist movement in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I believe we should not give too much importance to that situation. However, I would like, in a few words, to try and clarify the matter for the information of my English speaking friends who represent ridings in other provinces.
In the last century the province of Quebec had a population of farmers and craftsmen. It was only in the last generation that Quebec started to become an industrial province. Such a deep transformation creates a number of problems. At the present time, with the changes the premier of Quebec, Hon. Jean


Lesage, is bringing about, especially in the field of education, thousands of young French Canadians will soon make their entry on the labour market while thousands of university graduates will start their active life, and they will all ask for adequate employment.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those qualified young men want to have their due place in a French Canadian community and in the community of the province of Quebec as a whole.
As a French Canadian, I must admit that we all have a place in this house. We may speak French or English here and we enjoy complete freedom. But, unfortunately, I find that in the past French Canadians in the province of Quebec were too often left in the background, more particularly in the industrial and commercial field.
Today, we are able to carry out some functions competently. But unfortunately some industrialists and businessmen in Quebec have but too often failed to be frank and honest enough or were prejudiced against their French speaking fellow citizens, to the point of limiting their progress to a certain level. However, at this time, I have to render due tribute to various financial, commercial and industrial institutions in the province of Quebec, which offer to Canadians of French origin more and more possibilities for an advancement, to which they, indeed, have a right.
As a matter of fact, La Presse of Saturday, May 11, 1963, reproduced an item published in the Financial Post and stating that French had become the fashion in Montreal and that, if industrialists in the province of Quebec began to offer possibilities of advancement to French Canadians, it was due to a recognition of the latter's increased competence and present economic strength, which had to be reckoned with, as well as of the need to negotiate with those people. That is why many corporations in the province of Quebec now offer some possibilities of advancement to French speaking Canadians. I hope this trend will develop more and more in the years to come, so that we may live in peace within the Canadian confederation, as we trust we shall.
Mr. Speaker, we may, of course, pass some legislation in this house. However, the Canadian people in general, and more particularly the English speaking Canadians, should, in the province of Quebec as in the other provinces, give French Canadians the same possibilities of progress so that there would be no such discrimination as has been noted in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the present separatist movement is not serious. On the other hand, I feel that at the last federal election, the people of Quebec showed their trust in the party that has always recognized the importance of the French Canadians. That explains why so many ridings in Quebec have elected Liberals to represent them in this house, even though no expert could have forecast a Liberal victory in that province. It must be admitted that Quebec, in these times of confusion, has put her trust in the Liberal party, and it is the Liberal party which will restore a climate of confidence in the province of Quebec.

The mandate of the government elected by the people is to guide, through a vigorous impulse, the national economy, while leaving the greatest latitude to private enterprise and individuals so that they may play their proper part. Moreover, it should be well understood that the solution of our present problems depends more than ever on each and every one of us. To my mind, the state has to play a complementary part, that is to say it must provide that which our various organizations may be lacking, but it should not replace our institutions which, in spite of some statements to the contrary, have played a very useful and very important part in our economy, and which will yet be called upon to play a very important part in the raising of our standard of living.
As I am a farmer and therefore one of the rare representatives of that profession from the province of Quebec, I would like, at this point of my remarks, to speak about agriculture. Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to speak about the Quebec farmer, for he is a progressive fellow, a man who knows exactly where he is heading.
In days gone by, it was the fashion to dwell on his individualistic traits. Today it is evident that though he may be an individualist, he has learned to fully appreciate the virtues of a co-operation which helps him solve the problems of his rural community and improve its lot.
Since the last war, we are witnessing a technical and economic revolution, which
The Address-Mr. Vincent needs the farmer in order to succeed. The farmer has already benefited from that revolution; unfortunately, he also suffered from it.
In agricultural regions where revenues are insufficient to ensure a decent standard of living, farmers are indirectly prevented from investing in order to modernize their farms and take advantage of economic and technical progress.
These farmers, as well as those who live in more prosperous areas, do not intend to bow under the burden of the agricultural problem. They know that new problems call for new solutions and that people must sometimes aim at larger fields of action to find them.
They have won the confidence of the Canadian government from 1957 to 1963. That is why that government, as suggested by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), whose ability is well known, established a legislation entitled Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. The Canadian government of that time never intended to interfere in any way with the farmers' liberty of action. That legislation aimed only at giving them the technical and financial assistance which would enable them to put their good will, their ability and their social and professional organizations at the service of an idea, our agricultural survival.
As everyone knows, the federal government, on October 15 last, signed an agreement with the Quebec government.
When we lost power on April 22 last, great strides were being made in the province of Quebec. Many programs were in progress and many others were arranged for next summer.

Our party proposed a plan that would give complete medical care to everyone. We do not think the quality of medical care should

be determined by how much a person can afford. Rather, this should be determined only by the degree of illness. We believe that any plan of medicare must be all inclusive and completely comprehensive. It must include doctors' care, hospital care, dental care, drugs, glasses and other necessary appliances. This plan would be for the benefit of the people and not one designed against the doctors-after all, I am one myself. It would be designed to meet these needs without the sacrifice of the doctor-patient relationship. Doctors would be paid on a fee for service basis rather than a salary. This would maintain a doctor's incentive. He would have the complete freedom to practise inside or outside the plan and also have complete freedom of choice of his patients. This would be completely democratic and yet maintain the dignity and pride of the medical profession which it so justly deserves, because of its sacrifices and unswerving loyalty to the ailing since the ancient inception of this profession.
We feel, too, that the people are equally deserving of the best care available. Through experience in the practice of medicine I find there is a large group of people who are medically indigent. Some of these people have sufficient to make them ineligible for medical welfare assistance, yet they can ill afford adequate medical care. There are new discoveries in treatment, in newly derived drugs that cannot be used on as high a percentage of patients as they should be. The exorbitant prices of these drugs makes it necessary for doctors to substitute cheaper ones rather than use the best in the case of many of his patients. Because of financial obstacles, must our Canadian people receive second or third rate substitutions?
When a patient enters my office I am forced to make two diagnoses-one has to do with a medical diagnosis and the other with the patient's financial ability to pay for the treatment I will have to prescribe, whether it be drugs, surgery or even time off work that many can ill afford. What about private plans? These are so covered with exceptions, exclusions and fine print that to interpret them would take the ability of a legal man. None of these plans include dentistry or appliances. A few of them partially cover drugs on a percentage basis. It was interesting to note that in yesterday's Globe and Mail on the editorial page there was an editorial called "Facing the Inevitable", and I would like to read this.
The dental profession is showing wisdom in its co-operative and constructive approach to prepaid dental care. At the joint annual conventions of the Canadian and Ontario Dental Associations at the week end, it was disclosed that sponsoring
The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe
bodies had already been set up by the profession in British Columbia and Quebec to administer prepaid plans, and that similar bodies were in the process of formation in Alberta and Ontario. The Ontario group should be ready by the end of the year to administer plans on behalf of a number of groups.
Dr. W. G. McIntosh, past president of the Canadian Dental Association, had some words of advice for his colleagues. He warned them not to resist social change:
"The only reason for the existence of our profession is to serve others. If we fail to make our services available or place them beyond reach of the public, then our status as a profession and our legal power of self-regulation will quickly disappear .. . The cry of no government control is outdated. It is now a question of how much government control and how it can be most efficiently used in the best interests of all concerned." "
By moving voluntarily into the prepaid field, the dentists are co-operating gracefully with the inevitable. Dental bills place a greater financial burden on some families than medical bills, and there are many families who cannot afford dental care or for whom dental care is not available. The need is twofold: there should be prepaid plans that will spread the costs and enable people to guard against sudden and enormous bills by paying a reasonable monthly premium; and dental services should be made much more widely available.
These are not needs that can be quickly satisfied. The first plans put into operation in Ontario will be in the nature of experiments. Until they have been working for some time it will not be possible to determine the full extent of the need for dental services or to fix firm premiums. It is also probable that the original plans will function only in urban areas; the shortage of dentists in many rural communities at the present time could make any sort of comprehensive prepaid scheme impossible. Before prepaid dental service can be made available to all its citizens, Canada will need many more dentists.
The dentists are wise, however, in proceeding with their pilot schemes now. It is an indication of their recognition of the need, and of their willingness to co-operate in meeting it.
It is interesting to note that even the Globe and Mail does not speak in a derogatory way about the possibility of this plan being government run. Is it not the prime responsibility of any responsible government to attend to the health of the people?
Great Britain has had a medical plan since 1948, and although the Labour party, which had the sagacity to institute this plan, has been out of power since 1951 the plan has not been withdrawn. Rather, the Tories have recently offered increased benefits. The doctors want it, the people want it and even the government wants it. If such a plan as this could be brought in during a period of austerity in Britain by a Labour party, and not removed by governments following them, surely Canada is in a better position than Britain was in post-war days to institute a plan of similar magnitude for our Canadian people?
The complaint that quality would be substituted by quantity is unjustified, as evidenced by the Norwegian health plan. Two of the standards used for the determination of

The Address-Mr. Brown quality of medical practice are the infant mortality rate and the average life expectancy at birth. Both of these are considerably more favourable in Norway than either here or in the United States. Although medical education in Norway is free, there are still fewer doctors per capita and therefore the improved statistics are not explainable on the ground that Norwegian doctors handle fewer patients.
There are only two countries in the western world which have not achieved some form of government operated medical health plan __the United States and Canada. This is something the people need and want. I feel that a speech from the throne which omits even to mention this subject is remiss in attending to the needs of the people. Is this not truly the duty of a duly elected government? The people are not asking to be branded by the stigma of receiving charity from either the government or other people but I do feel that anyone who is doing a job to the fullest of his ability should have equal rights and access to benefits available to everyone; he should not be looked upon as seeking charity, but, rather, recognized as a human being, not indigent but with equal rights. If any one right falls in this category it is the right to health.
A properly planned medical health scheme that is truly all-inclusive would advance the course of medical science, because it would not only look after the people but it would provide incentive to the doctors and advance the cause of scientific research without such duplication of effort as results today from the studies of private companies. It would make the latest scientific advances available to anyone whose medical condition required them. This would be the only criterion of their use, as the financial barrier would be removed. Also, education along medical lines would be made available to those who have the ability. Today, one needs both ability and opportunity. This would make the opportunity available to all those who have the ability.
Only through idealism is the realism of improvement accomplished. A goal set high remains an eternal objective even if never attained. Perfection is impossible to attain, but the closer we can come to it the better will be the life of our people. So, let us all work and build a new Canada with standards for our people that will be the envy of the world.

The potentialities of the Grand river were recognized from earliest times by both wise Indians and white men alike. It traces a majestic course from its source in central Ontario to its mouth at lake Erie. It was at the fall of the river, which is also the ford of the river, to where the earliest white settlers in the area came. This river valley was chosen by the Indians of the Six Nations when they settled in Canada following the American revolution under their redoubtable chief Joseph Brant, that illustrious leader of men, both Indians and whites alike, and a valiant ally of the British crown. And as
The Address-Mr. Brown I said, the earliest white men followed Joseph Brant to settle at the ford of the river, at Brant's ford, there to establish the beginnings of the province of Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, did you know that when Brantford was a port whole families of people came from as far away as Virginia, bringing their slaves with them to spend their summers in the delightful climate of our part of Ontario? The historic Kerby hotel at Brantford was jammed to the doors every summer in the 1850's, and they had to set up an annex across the river to hold the crowds.
What I am saying is that this great river must be made navigable for the reasons I will outline. Did you know, Mr. Speaker, that in the last few years every municipality along the Grand river has spent large sums of money, some in the millions, establishing sewage disposal plants, with the help and direction of the provincial government, in order to put an end to the pollution of the river? The result is that it is rapidly being restored to its pristine beauty-to its old and rightful place in the life of all those important communities on its banks. It is being made ready for navigation again, and the federal government, this government will, I know, be called upon to give a little leadership in restoring navigation.
Perhaps commercial navigation may never develop again on the river-who knows? But navigation for pleasure craft will change the entire economic life of this whole area. The possibilities for recreation in the valley of the Grand, serving the whole area between what is called the Golden Horseshoe around lake Ontario and down to the region of lake Erie, are unlimited.
Hon. members will be well aware of the increased interest in boating and water sports over the last few years. The highways in our part of Ontario are full of people hauling boats either to Georgian bay or lake Erie. This should not be necessary when all they have to do is put their craft on the water at Brantford. Further down the river past the Six Nations Indian reservation and Chiefs-wood, the newly restored home of the Indian poetess, Pauline Johnson, is Caledonia, where above the dam the boating and water sports enjoyed are a sight to see.
With some dredging and a number of low dams, the entire Grand river and its flat lands on either side will become, in my view, a recreational area second to none in North America and serving a whole number of communities throughout its length, in the most densely populated parts of Canada.
With the river pollution coming to an end, with help from the federal government to

The Address-Mr. Korchinski promote navigation, and with the construction of certain small sized dams, the adjoining farm lands, always a credit to our province, will be enhanced in value by the possibility of irrigation, so that agriculture will be able to hold its accustomed place as a cornerstone of the economy of the Grand valley.
The redevelopment of the Grand river will also be one of those projects which the federal government can promote at this particular time, or in the near future, to alleviate the unemployment problem in the area. It is a public project that will bring about a good return on the investment made. There will be resultant prosperity ensuing from the establishment of this enviable recreational area, one which will be second to none in Canada.
Millions of dollars have been spent in past years on the Trent valley system and on the Rideau canal system, and I believe, and believe firmly, that the next great move on the part of government will be the redevelopment of the Grand river for navigation. Present day urban civilization requires a multiplicity of parklands and recreational areas, and the potential of the Grand river valley is tremendous in this respect.
As I said at the outset, great men of the past recognized its value and potential by settling there. Joseph Brant and the chiefs of the Indians of the Six Nations confederacy, after careful study, chose this area as above all a place worthy to establish in the wilderness a haven where British justice under the crown of England would flourish and prevail.
The white man, after the advent of railways, rather carelessly neglected some of our splendid waterways, including the Grand river. Today his descendants are turning to these rivers again for recreation and the Grand river area will, I confidently predict, from one end to the other become a retreat for countless thousands and a bulwark against the pressures of modern urban civilization.

Mr. Deputy Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, like so many others I would first like to congratulate you on your election to the office you hold. We heard them say: "It is time for action; it is time we got a new government." But what do we find in the speech from the throne? They have copied it, and I admire them for doing that. I am glad they could see the wisdom in the legislation we had presented.
We left the country in a better position than the press, Liberal spokesmen and television commentators made it appear. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, quite a hoax was perpetrated on the Canadian people. I have before me a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of May 1 and under the heading, "A house left in good order" there appears this:
Official figures which came last week should be noted well by Canadians.
For what they showed, beyond any dispute whatever, is that when Mr. Diefenbaker last week handed over the government of Canada to Mr. Pearson he presented Mr. Pearson with a house in good order.

The Address-Mr. Korchinski
Let us go on. Will we have a repetition of the same mistakes, only to get the same answers? speechtext: I have heard about the timber board and all the timber board did was to lay off people in that area at a time when the N.D.P. were crying about unemployment. People have talked to me about it. Is it any wonder that people who know about the timber board will not support their party?

speechtext:
The situation in Saskatchewan is well known and certainly the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam should be quite well aware of that fact because the people indicated in no uncertain terms a year ago what they thought of that type of planning.
I come now to the municipal development board. This is merely an extension of legislation now in effect with regard to sewer and water programs. There will be a forgiveness clause. How long is the period to be? Nobody knows. There is nothing wrong with that type of legislation but it is repetition. Where is the bold new action we were led to believe would come from the Liberal party? There is nothing.
The provision for an economic council for Canada is just another name for the national productivity council. Again I say that all the Liberals will do will be to make new appointments and put a new man at the head of it. Perhaps some of their candidates who were not successful will be on that board. They were unsuccessful in one place but they will put them in another place, to make a success.
Contributory pensions are another idea that we had. They told us in the last session of parliament that their one big aim was to destroy a government that had nothing to offer, and yet they are offering the very things we did. Where is that bold new action? It is not coming and will not come from them. No.
They tell us that in a few years we will have a new flag. I wonder whether on his recent trip south the Prime Minister of Canada discussed this matter with the president and

The Address-Mr. Korchinski decided that perhaps one more star on their flag would be the solution. Is there agreement in this regard? After all, there seems to be agreement on everything else. It would appear from all the commentators in the press and on the radio that we have reached a wonderful Utopia. Just one little trip to the south and everything is fine.
As a matter of fact, I came through the United States myself when I drove to Ottawa. There is nothing wrong with going there, but to think that we will get all the answers because we have a new Prime Minister who cannot say no to anything seems to me to be stretching the imagination pretty far. The throne speech has been called imaginative, but you have to stretch your imagination to see what is in it that is new. Nothing, I say. After all, the flag of the country to the south has flown over military installations in this country in the past. There was nothing wrong with money from that country coming to Liberal headquarters during the campaign. That was wonderful. They had every assistance on television and in the press, all across Canada. To what avail? They could not convince the people, even with all their money. It is entirely up to the United States as to what they want to do, but I understand they want to have a member in this house, somebody to be their spokesman. Apparently the ambassadors are to sit on the sidelines. I understand that Congressman Hays has introduced a bill to this effect, which also makes provision for Canadian representation in their legislative bodies. Can you imagine Canada having an effective voice in their house of representatives and senate? Their spokesman would have every right to come into the Canadian House of Commons, tell us what they believe and perhaps give us an indication of what is necessary for Canada. Wonderful.
Now we come to some of the new ideas in the throne speech. One of them is to have two ministers of agriculture. I think it would be a good idea to have a lot of ministers of agriculture. That is evident from some of the experiences we have had in the last couple of days. I think the Prime Minister should have asked the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) one thing: "Have you read the agricultural platform of the Liberal party?" In that way he would prepare himself for the type of questions that may be asked him. I am sure he has no idea, as is evident, of what is in that platform; if there is a platform; but they did put out some material it would be very nice if he had read it.
I asked a question the other day: What is the higher initial price for oats and barley? It was taken as notice. I have just had a phone call. Seeding is almost finished and I should like to know what that higher price for oats


and barley is. The former minister of agriculture rose today and told us that the price of barley has gone down. What did their platform mean? Is that not perpetrating a hoax? What were they trying to tell the people of the west? Is it any wonder they have so few members from the west? I have a pamphlet here issued by the Liberal party, and do you know what it says? "Ensure a minimum return on wheat". I emphasize the word "minimum" because that is exactly what we are heading for. It says "minimum".
Why do we need two ministers of agriculture? Would it be because they wish to have somebody to whom they can pass the buck? Whenever you do not want to make a decision, you hand it over to the other man.
Just a few minutes ago there were two members talking behind the curtains. They were both talking about sugar beets, but one was from Ontario and one was from Alberta. Who will look after the problem? How are you going to solve that? What about hogs? What about eggs? What about cattle? What about grain, for example, that will be sold in the east and grown in the west? Who is supposed to decide that problem? Where do we go? Is this an admission by the Liberals that they cannot possibly handle the problems with one minister? Already, they have taken the wheat board away from the department of agriculture. We used to have one minister who did a remarkable job. We had one of the greatest ministers of agriculture Canada ever had. The Liberals are admitting that they cannot handle these problems, so they take the wheat board away from the Minister of Agriculture. Then, they will split the remainder of the responsibilities in half. I understand, too, that they are supposed to set up another cabinet minister to deal with Saskatchewan. Then, there is supposed to be another committee. What are we going to have, Mr. Speaker? Who is supposed to be charged with these responsibilities? To whom do I go in the event that there are problems?- and there will be many agricultural problems, according to evidence already produced.
One of the first acts of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) was to reduce the price support on whole milk. I saw an article in the Ottawa Citizen of May 22 entitled, "Bread price rise may follow milk." It reads:
Rising prices of powdered milk across Canada could lead to higher prices for bread, dairy industry spokesmen say ...
The milk powder increases were sparked by the removal of a federal government subsidy to farmers of 25 cents for 100 pounds of whole milk.
To whom do I go with a problem like that? Already, it is evident that we cannot get answers. It is evident that there will be problems, and to whom do we go? A strange new

animal is going to make its appearance here, something with two heads. The other day the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) asked a question of the minister. What kind of answer did he get? He was informed that the new plan for the Department of Agriculture would save the treasury some $6 million. This is the first aim, to save the treasury money and forget about the farmers. They want to forget about the farmers, whether they are from the east or the west. Perhaps this is what the Prime Minister meant when he spoke in New Brunswick and said they were not going to spend a single nickel. Is this what he was referring to, that they were not going to cut off all grants?
We had the acreage payment, and what do we get? There was a promise of $2 per bushel for wheat. Apparently, however, this does not have the priority to be included within the 60 days of decision. When will it be included, Mr. Speaker, if ever? What are we supposed to do? Are we to wait until just before another election, only to find they will use that same old bribe? I can remember the years when they pitted the east against the west. During the last five or six years, we have been able to smooth this over. In other words, we have put the farmers in a position where for once they have had a fair share of attention given to them. The Liberals are putting us right back into that old position. They are doing this because they have only one thing in mind, to hang on to power. Since Saskatchewan did not give them any representatives, they will go in a roundabout way to see what they can do to get a few members from that area. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that they have a lot to learn.
The other day they sent an invitation to one of our more illustrious members, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), to sit on their side of the house. I can assure them he will teach them plenty. He has done a terrific job in bringing to the government's attention the needs of his constituency. I can assure the Liberals that if they would take the time to read some of the literature that has been published, such as the brief put out by the farmers' union, they would learn something. They offer us nothing but two heads for agriculture. The farmers had better be satisfied with that.
We are told the government will establish a ministry of industry which is supposed to solve the problems of industry. What will it do for my constituency? I have already pointed out the potentials existing in my area. We have mines, we have timber, we have water, we have good farmland and we have the people. If the government just deals with the areas of chronic unemployment, they will just deal with Toronto. They will
The Address-Mr. Korchinski deal with the cities because those are the areas in which chronic unemployment is evident. Will they concern themselves with other areas? Will they try to boost the economy of other areas? They will not, because that does not have priority. The Prime Minister has said that the best way to prosperity for farmers throughout the country is through the expansion of markets at home and abroad. Is it any wonder that he needs two ministers of agriculture? I think he will keep one at home and he will send the other one on a trip. I suggest that if he is going to send any minister of agriculture on a trip, he should send the present one, because obviously we have not had an indication from this minister that there will be $2 wheat or that there will be an increase in the initial price of oats and barley, or other legislation. The only indication we have received is that there will be an expansion of the Department of Agriculture. We are going to have more ministers, more secretaries and so on. This is supposed to solve the unemployment problem.
One of the things that was evident under the former administration was that the western farmers were getting their fair share of attention. One of the things that was evident was the amount of machinery the farmers were beginning to buy. I found over the last couple of years that the farmers were not grumbling as they had under the Liberal government. We managed to get them into a position where they received their share of attention. They were not unhappy over the fact the maritimes got its share of attention. They were not unhappy over the fact that eastern Canada got its share of attention. They were happy over the fact that for once they were getting their share of attention.
There was an article in the Winnipeg Tribune dated February 22, 1963 entitled "Western prosperity", and it read:
One of the indicators of relative farm prosperity is the statistics of farm implement sales. When farm income rises it is followed immediately by an increase in the consumption of goods of all kinds, particularly farm machinery.
According to figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics, sales of farm implements and equipment in 1962 were valued at wholesale prices as an estimated $279,019,000 or an increase over 1961 of 15.6 per cent. . .
There could hardly be a more concrete confirmation of the general proposition that the government's agricultural policies have benefited western Canada.
I should like the new government to take note of that because any time the western farmer gets his fair share of attention and is prosperous, that money will be channelled back into the east. We have been trying to remind the Liberals of this fact. Every time there is any indication the farmer might have

The Address-Mr. Korchinski a good crop, the agents will be on his doorstep to see what they can sell him. The farmer will buy just as he has in the past. This government should take note of that fact. Instead of running around setting up all kinds of ministers, I think they should get down to the basic problem of trying to put more money into the hands of the farmers. They should forget about playing politics and give the farmers the acreage payments, even if we did introduce them.
It is an odd thing, Mr. Speaker, but when we ask questions of the minister we do not get any replies. I cannot blame him if he does not have all the answers because this is a difficult department to administer and no doubt it is difficult for him to know all the answers. It is difficult to know all the answers, and we will not hold him to that. But here is one of the pamphlets put out by the Liberal party dealing with today's problems where they answer these problems. When will we get the answers? Do we have to wait for another throne speech to get some of the answers? We will never get them from this government.
What is going to happen if the decision of one minister on one course of action disagrees with the decision of the other minister? What are they going to do? Are they going to look around to see who gets more votes, or which has the biggest voting potential east or west. What about the maritimes? What about the people of British Columbia, the fruit producers? Mr. Speaker, I do not know how long I have been on my feet.

He is going to ignore that part of the country because there are not too many votes to be garnered there. They are not too concerned about that part of Canada. Do they think they will look after unemployment that way? One of their candidates said they were going to do something about roads to resources and roads to the north. What kind of a position does this put the candidates in from 

those areas? I am sure they must be somewhat ashamed of the manner in which the Liberal party is acting today in connection with those very things.
I have the pamphlets here. How can these candidates stand for the very things they thought their party leader would do for them? How can they answer these charges? They cannot, because it is impossible to do so. The Liberal party just does not do anything, period. That is exactly what they have been noted for in the past. This has been their theme for years. They will offer a little carrot here and perhaps talk about these things. Biculturalism is a wonderful thing. I think I have almost as many people in my constituency from different countries and of different nationalities as any hon. member. I think these people are interested in living together, because they have proved in the past that they can live together. But the Liberal party at election times just offers a little carrot here and there in order to get votes.
What about the scholarships which they promised? If this is supposed to solve part of the unemployment problem, why is there no mention of scholarships? They ignore that. Perhaps we will hear about scholarships before the next election. According to the speech from the throne one of the greatest problems in Canada today is unemployment. If unemployment is one of the greatest problems-and I assure the house that it is a problem-why are there not two ministers of labour? Why did they ignore labour in this respect? If they think that agriculture needs the attention of two ministers, why not appoint two ministers to deal with the problems of labour? It seems to me the only reason they are trying to give agriculture that type of attention is because they were sadly lacking in votes in agriculture areas. If so many people are suffering as the result of unemployment, I suggest to the Prime Minister that instead of filling his cabinet with unnecessary members he should appoint two ministers of labour, one for employment and one for unemployment, if he wishes.
