speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, like others before me I should like to congratulate you upon election to your high office, and through you I should like to extend my congratulations to the Speaker. I know that both of you will show the ability, integrity and impartiality of your high office in administering the affairs of this house.
The leader of the Social Credit party decried the fact that we talk politics in this House of Commons. This is the place where we should talk politics. But we should at least be agreed, not only upon our Speaker and his impartiality but upon many of the facts which are often in dispute. Among these I would include facts as to economic realities. The speech from the throne contains the proposal that this parliament pass legislation with respect to a national economic council. We need a national economic council in this country in order to determine what the current trends are. The council may make forecasts of various kinds, but these forecasts are merely an indication of what basic, underlying trends and forces are currently at work in our economy.
This national economic council must not be a secretive body. It must work with agencies, particularly economic research groups, representatives of management and representatives of trade unions. It must communicate freely and frequently with them. I would argue that it should be staffed in large part by men who are seconded for relatively short periods of time from management and labour. In that way the government would certainly be better informed, and industry, management and labour would know to a much greater extent where we are going. If where we are going does not satisfy management, industry and labour, then we obviously have to change things. But at least these trends will be clearly mapped out. We will not be
The Address-Mr. Davis arguing much about what has happened in the distant past or what is happening currently, but more about where we should be going and what should be done with respect to redirecting our economy in ways we think are most desirable.
In other words, we should be arguing more about long term goals and objectives, more about policy, more about politics in the sense of the fundamental shape of the Canadian economy and our nation in the years to come.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is pretty good now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We need long term forecasting and long term planning, because at the moment we are looking ahead essentially a year at a time. Our annual budgets merely look ahead one year, but many investments made by individuals and industry are in assets, buildings and equipment which will last, not five or ten years, but 25, 50 years or even a century.
In order to make decisions intelligently we must be looking ahead not just one year but much further into the future, and the national economic development council will help us to do just that. It will remove a lot of uncertainties. Government will not be introducing policies and legislation whose provisions conflict with each other. Industries and individuals throughout this country will know better where they are going and what alternatives are open to them. They will be able to make their own decisions and invest in the light of the best possible information.
Also in the speech from the throne is a proposal for the setting up of a new department of industry. We have had traditionally in this country a Department of Trade and Commerce nominally, at least, concerned with international trade. More recently we have had a Department of Defence Production concerned primarily with buying munitions of war for our armed forces. But many of the decisions taken by these departments have influenced industry in this country. The setting up of a new department of industry will enable us to deal more directly and more frankly with industrial development in Canada.
The Glassco commission recommended the establishment of a purchasing department incorporating the Department of Defence Production. The new department of industry will be more than that. It will be a department whose actions, contracts and placement of requirements will influence industry to an undoubted extent, but within an over-all framework of flexible targets and long term objectives.
Economic research is one thing, but in addition to economic research we should do

The Address-Mr. Davis a great deal more scientific and basic research. We do not do much of the latter at the present time. The new department of industry will help to stimulate scientific and industrial research. It could do so in various ways, through tax incentives and so on.
I personally think we would be well advised to make Canada a tax haven in respect of research and development of various kinds. We should define research broadly and should free from the imposition of income tax the results of research, particularly royalties and revenues from the sale of what are essentially ideas. This would not only encourage the development of new industries in this country but it would cause some large international corporations, which so far have been very shy about carrying out any research here, to do so in the future.
Think of what this would mean in terms of employment for scientifically trained people, particularly for our youth. This is an area in which we have little to lose because at the present time we do not gain much from these activities. This is the type of activity which I sincerely hope the new department will encourage as part of a comprehensive program of revitalizing our country and increasing the opportunities of ownership in industry in Canada. I mention ownership because ownership generally follows ideas. The people who create new ideas are generally on the inside track. It is where research is done and where management is aware of the opportunities offered by scientific research that one finds opportunities to hold the equity control of new companies. I think this is important for Canada's future, particularly as the trend for many years now has been toward increased foreign ownership. This is one of the more positive and more liberal ways of increasing Canadian ownership in Canadian industry.
The new department of industry will have under its jurisdiction the national development corporation. This corporation will provide funds for the creation of certain new industries in circumstances where private enterprise does not, at least as yet, see its way clear to establish industries without substantial subsidy. I can think of various projects which I, personally, would like to see launched and I am sure every other hon. member has other projects in mind which he considers are on the verge of being economic propositions. Some of these could be accelerated if the government got into the picture at an early stage. One scheme which I have been pushing for years concerns the processing of uranium in this country to convert it into forms which are useable overseas in a variety of applications-power plants, submarines, cargo ships and so on. At present

we only produce raw natural uranium. We should be able to convert it into a more saleable form. Today, we are unable to sell a large part of our uranium production in its natural state. We would have to sell it to the United States atomic energy commission, and that commission is following a policy of making the United States self-sufficient in respect of uranium supplies. In other words, we cannot sell to the United States and we cannot process the product here.
I am not advocating the creation of large numbers of crown corporations one after the other. I think they might well be created at times but, surely, relatively low cost money is a sufficient advantage. It must be remembered that the majority of these corporations operate free of taxes in various respects and, certainly, free of income tax. Thus they enjoy a great advantage over the private sector of the economy.
If we go on in this way, if we continue this immense financial bias in the creation of crown companies we shall eventually arrive at the creation of a socialistic state north of the international boundary. I think we should develop a mechanism for selling off these crown corporations. This has been done in other parts of the world. West Germany, for example, sold the Volkswagen factory in such a way that the people were able to participate in its ownership. Shares were distributed in various areas in Germany and a tax incentive is still provided, all of which has ensured that the company is largely in the hands of West German nationals. I think we could devise ways in Canada of getting government out of business as well as into business, as well as ways of creating Canadian ownership and retaining ownership in this country. This is essential, and we need effective arrangements of this kind if, in fact, we are going to buy back a substantial amount of the ownership of industry within this great nation of ours.
I must insist on this: in order to grow we must also change, and in the process of change certain industries are bound eventually to decline; they must make way for newer and more vital industries. In speeches in our chambers of commerce the emphasis has always been on growth-on the growing industries rather than on the declining industries, those which have to receive government support in the form of subsidies and so on. Provision has been made for tremendous subsidies to the coal mining industry, for example. At the other extreme we are subsidizing nuclear power, which is not yet an economic proposition. At the same time we are heavily taxing the truly economic industries of oil and gas and, to a lesser extent, hydroelectric power. This is not the

way to improve the economy of the country unless, taking the long view, we are consciously allowing the old and less economic industries to die. One of the best ways of letting them die is to leave them in the private sector.
I believe we need more economic information, particularly economic information of a long term, fundamental type. But we must leave the policy-making essentially to the politicians, in other words to the members of this chamber, and have those policies debated in this chamber. We do need planning, but we do not have to be set inevitably on a course towards a collectivist state. I am a small "1" liberal. But I am also a big "L" Liberal in that I believe that at this time we have in the Liberal party the most effective team for bringing about a true nation with a true national identity and the maximum freedom for the individual in this country. I do not believe in buying the voter with his own taxes. I do not believe in running a continuous deficit in our budgets, because I believe that this is merely postponing to the future the shouldering of an immense financial burden. I believe it is merely confusing the individual Canadians of this country as to the course of events, if we do not lay long term policies before them but are merely borrowing on tomorrow and paying them subsidies and supports of one kind or another. In that way we are plunging inevitably toward some sort of collectivist state, and that is the main reason why I had no confidence in the Conservative party last year during the twenty fifth parliament.
We also have a tremendous deficit in our international balance of payments, a state of affairs which has existed for a number of years. This amounted to a substantial sum in the early fifties and it has continued in the last half dozen years. This, put in the most summary terms, means that we have been living beyond our means, that we have been borrowing from others. We have been able to borrow only because we mortgaged the resources and the ownership of industry in this country. We must not confuse the people any more. We must indicate, first, through long term economic projections, and then through distasteful policies, if necessary, what the alternatives are and what course we must follow if we are not only to balance our own budget internally but also to balance the budget we have with other countries, so as to buy back our inheritance and be independent, and really achieve this true north, strong and free.
The basic burden of my remarks this afternoon is essentially this. We need to look ahead. We need to go forward in the sense
The Address-Mr. Lambert of knowing a little more what is happening, what the fundamental forces at work today are, and where we are going if we do not consciously change course and set our sails toward the objective which we all agree is desirable. We need good communications, and good communications mean at least a national economic council and a department of industry which will carry out a number of tasks which industry needs to perform, including industrial research and development. The speech from the throne was only the beginning, but I believe we have started on our way. I believe we are beginning to raise our eyes and look ahead, and for this reason, Mr. Speaker, I trust we will find tonight a majority in this house in support of the government.

Before I turn to the speech from the throne I should like to acknowledge the support I have received from my constituency of Edmonton West.
Hon. members may not realize this. After all the press on numerous occasions has indicated, and not only the press but people who have some lack of knowledge about western Canada, that western Canada is composed only of rural constituencies and that the members on this side of the house

who adhere to the Conservative party represent only agrarian constituencies. That is far from the case.
It may be of interest to the house to know that the constituency I represent is either the seventh or eighth most populous in the country, and is closely followed by two constituencies in Calgary and another in Edmon-ton-Strathcona. As a matter of fact, the three Edmonton constituencies are just as urban as almost any other in the country. Therefore, the fact that the three Edmonton constituencies are represented by members of the Progressive Conservative party, together with two constituencies in Calgary-and we were not too far off making a clean sweep in Calgary -would show it is inaccurate to state that it was only the farmers of western Canada who supported the Conservative party. Western Canada as a whole did that.
It may be, as someone has said, that some of the eastern dailies did not get out there. Certainly they did not have many people out there to survey the scene and, if I may introduce a personal note, those who did come, as in 1962, in 1963 said I was one of those people earmarked for sure defeat by some prime candidate of the Liberal party. I think these commentators, when they came out west, used to go into Calgary. I do not know what form of ouija board they consulted, but they always forecast that I was going to be the loser. The people of Edmonton West did not share that opinion.
As a matter of fact this time not only did the Liberals send in a lot of party bigwigs- I think we had the visitations of even the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) and a few others-but we also had what I would consider the biggest flood of eastern Liberal money the west has ever seen. We all know the money had to be raised elsewhere because they were not raising it locally; but the net result was that my majority this time was doubled, and all the majorities of my colleagues in and about Edmonton were also increased. So, I say, let them send all the money they want and let them send the same people to visit the west and we are assured of being re-elected again.
The hon. member for Northumberland would have been far more effective if she had been supporting the type of speech which we had been led to expect, by the beating of bands and the sounding of trumpets prior to the opening of parliament. We were led to believe that this was going to be the speech of all speeches, that this was going to be the program that was to be the ultimate of all programs. The economy of Canada was to be

got going again. Well, Mr. Speaker, how can you get something going unless it had been previously stopped? I am sure there is not one hon. member opposite who will dare support the proposition that Canada's economy had slowed down to the point that it was almost stopped, because statistics-any kind at which they want to look-will absolutely refute that assertion.
I seem to recall that in 1962 the members of the opposition, and those people who supported them in the press, were forecasting a dire future for Canada. In May and June of 1962 they said we were going completely to the dogs, that our trade was going to be wiped away and we were heading for depression-mind you, not recession but depression. They also said the cost of living was going to zoom upwards. They did not mention that once in 1963.
We can look at the record in trade. 1 shall not give the figures because they have all been put on the record in the last few days. However, I shall refer to them briefly. It seems to me the Liberal party has suddenly discovered that Canada has got a deficit on its balance of international payments, but I ask when did Canada not have one? They seem to think this is a recent discovery, but I would point out in the matter of commodity trade, tremendous strides had been made, not by the former government but under the aegis of the government. They were made by Canadian business, by Canadian businessmen who did not believe those opposition forebodings of last year. Instead they went out and beat all records. The same is true of heavy industry which went out and beat the records of previous years. People in heavy industry did not believe the Liberal party, the New Democratic party or the Social Credit party. This in itself is a tribute to Canadian businessmen and industry.
Our industrial program has kept pace all the way along in 1963. If there was going to be a recession, 1962 was a flash in the pan. Steel and automobile production are up, and let me assure hon. gentlemen on the other side that the sales of automobiles back in January, February and March long predated any question that Liberals would form a minority administration. Record sales of automobiles are not a May wonder of 1963.
In addition, the cost of living has maintained an even keel, with a very minor advance, again showing that the forecasts, estimates and guesstimates of those experts, or so-called experts, of 1962 were very wrong.
What do they mean by "getting the economy going again"? I think it is just a mere slogan, something that has been borrowed from some other book. This was a catch phrase on another occasion, so let us not
The Address-Mr. Lambert hear any more about getting the economy rolling or going again. Let them maintain the momentum. Then we will listen to government spokesmen; but let us not hear any more about getting it rolling again. Maintain the momentum and let it go forward.

The Address-Mr. Hahn
I stand here in this assembly making my maiden speech, and I confess to the usual amount of nervousness that most new members must feel. However, I also confess to a feeling of pride. I, like everybody here, am proud to be a Canadian. As a Canadian, I am particularly proud to be able to stand in this house, the greatest of our Canadian institutions, and represent the people of my constituency. As a member of this institution, I am proud that I am standing on this side of the house supporting the new Liberal government, for I strongly feel that this government will be a great government.
As a new member, Mr. Speaker, I come to this house with a certain amount of idealism about it, with a certain amount of respect for the institution. I know that the last session of parliament has been discussed by many who felt it was not up to the mark. Since I have been here I have heard comments, particularly from some hon. members on the other side of the house, concerning the failures, and the causes of the failures of the last parliament. I have heard suggestions given, primarily to us on the government side, about what might be done to rectify the situation. Perhaps it is impertinent for me, as a new member, to discuss these things, but having sat here and listened to the things that have been said I feel, first of all, that I cannot help agreeing with many of the things that have been said from the other side of the house.
However, it seems to me that some things have been left unsaid. As I have said previously, we have a responsibility to recognize the rights of minority parties, to recognize the importance of parliament. However, I believe hon. gentlemen opposite must realize there are two sides to the question. There are two sides to this house. They, too, have a responsibility. They have the responsibility to conduct their opposition vigorously and to the best of their ability; but I think that all of us must bear in mind that we are here, not to continue the last election campaign but to conduct the nation's business. I think that if members on both sides of the house will recognize this, then, at the end of our first session, we new members will have kept our respect and idealism.

Mr. Speaker, before the recess I had completed my introductions and would now like to move on to the main points which I should like to discuss. My riding is Broadview, which is a downtown Toronto

riding. Most of the people in my riding depend either directly or indirectly on industry for their livelihood. To my constituents unemployment is a very real, critical problem. Throughout the campaign and since, many, many people have come to me with the problem of finding a job. There is not much point talking to these people about the booming conditions in our economy because to them it does not mean very much. While the figures that have been cited in this house do indicate that we have made progress in the last year, we still have not solved this most critical of problems. So that if I talk of boom to my people, they talk to me about jobs.
We all know that unemployment is probably the worst blight on our society. We all know what unemployment does to the selfesteem of a man who wants to work but who is rejected time after time. We know we cannot let this continue. We also know that while we have unemployment we cannot do many of the other things that we want to do for our people. There is no magic wand. Our economy cannot support advanced social measures while it is supporting a large number of people who should be working. It is imperative that this problem be recognized, that it be tackled and tackled effectively. I believe, from the measures I have seen in the speech from the throne, that our government is going to do just that.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to outline the basis of the problem as I see it and then show what I think we can do about it. First of all, where do the jobs come from? Over the next few years we have to find large numbers of new jobs each year. Where do we find them? I think we also know that most jobs must come from industry. Therefore if we are going to create new jobs, this is the area to which we must look. We know that in order to expand our industry we have to produce some of the things that we are now consuming but which we are bringing in from outside our country. We also know that probably one fifth of our jobs depend on exports. Therefore as our jobs must grow, so must we increase our exports.
How are we equipped now to do that job? What is the condition of our industry? I think we all know that you can sell a product either because it is cheap and competitively priced, or because it is of a unique design that nobody else has. These are the two criteria upon which you can make sales.
In Canada our manufacturers are generally producing for the Canadian market, a market of 18 million people. This is a low volume. Yet our wage structure is high in relation to our European competitors, and it is close to

that of our competitor to the south. We therefore have a situation of relatively high wage costs and low volumes of production. The two together mean that our costs are high.
What about our ability to design our own products and produce unique designs? We are not doing it, by and large, because most of our companies are either subsidiaries of foreign concerns, using the design of their parent concern outside this country, or they are Canadian concerns that are buying its research and development through licensing agreements with foreign concerns. We in this country are not producing our own unique designs. So that we do not have either low cost or unique design.
If I may cite an example from my own experience, we were producing home laundry equipment. This was a product designed in the United States and we were working under a licensing agreement. In Canada we produced in one year what the United States concern produced in five days. How could we hope to take a carbon copy of their product and try and compete with them in export markets? This was an impossibility.
My predecessor from Broadview, the former minister of trade and commerce, was very active in trying to stimulate exports. I believe that the principles upon which his trade drives were based were sound, but I also feel that somehow the cart got ahead of the horse. We had built up a sales force and were trying to sell before we had products to put on the market, and before we had negotiated the necessary trade agreements so that we did have a market. These are difficult problems to solve, and anybody who claims he can solve them overnight or in 60 days is not basing his claim on realism.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the measures outlined in the speech from the throne will start the action necessary to effect the cures that we must have. I should like to look briefly at some of these measures. First of all, it has been said in this house that we have proposed nothing that will put people to work quickly. Well, I dispute that. The municipal loan fund is to me our shot in the arm, our shock treatment. It can and will put people to work quickly. That is one of its purposes. The type of things that will be done under this program are projects that can be
The Address-Mr. Hahn implemented and put into effect quite quickly. So that through the municipal loan fund we should be able to take up the slack, to put people to work, to get them to work in a hurry.
We also know that this is no long term cure. We know this will not solve the problem, because we know we must also increase our industry. This is why we are suggesting that we set up a department of industry. The department of industry will have the responsibility of solving what I call the technical problems that face us. It will have to tackle the problem of our high costs; it will have to tackle the problem of research and development in this country. It must also bring together management and labour so that instead of these two groups battling each other and treating each other with suspicion, as they have in the past, they will work together, realizing that their enemy is not each other but that they must join together and battle the common enemy of world competition around us.
We in Canada have the ability, the technical knowledge and the skill to do well in the area of research. I have only to point to the number of Beavers, Otters and Caribou flying around in the skies of the world to indicate what can be done by this country. While tax incentives may be one way of encouraging research they would be of little use, it seems to me, when a company would not realize the profit from its research work for a number of years, or in the case of a company without sufficient capital to launch a research project. I think some of the suggestions made by my hon. friend from Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) might be effective in dealing with this situation.
The new department of industry will have to look at the situation as our tariffs come down, and devise ways and means in which our industry can prepare itself to make an onslaught on world markets. This department could also produce some immediate short range benefits. During the election campaign the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) talked about what might be done in the automobile industry. The suggestions he had to make then could be applied in the case of many industries.
Let us take an example with which I am familiar, the home laundry equipment industry. We had a range of home laundry products consisting of 15 models with five different machine tops required for them. If we had received some direction from the government and knew our competitors were thinking along the same lines, we might have been able to reduce the volume of imported

The Address-Mr. Hahn parts considerably by cutting down the number of our model lines to perhaps seven or eight models and the number of machine tops required to probably two. On this basis we would have had sufficient volume to justify tooling up for the production of these tops in Canada. It would have provided employment for the tool and die shops, additional work in our factory and, perhaps, sufficient work for a porcelain enamel plant. If the government could encourage industry to take action of this kind, results would be produced in short order.
The creation of a department of industry will not solve our problems though it will create a mechanism through which they can be solved. We know we must expand our trade. I believe we all recognize the work being done by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) to set up, with the western nations, proper trading areas for us. It is useless for us in this country to resist the trends that are taking place around the world. We must join those trends and derive the maximum benefit from them. This is what is being done now.
To do the things we have to do will require money. We would normally expect that industry would provide its own financing. However, through the Canadian development corporation we also have a means of providing funds when traditional methods fail. I hope this corporation will halt the sale of our industry to foreign countries. I hope it will begin the process of buying back industry which has already been sold. I hope that by this means more capital may be provided for risk ventures. I know a number of people who have had ideas for good products but they did not have the capital to develop them; they had to take their ideas to the United States and have them developed there. I think we should be able to provide the risk capital here when it is needed for projects of this nature.
If we are to compete successfully in foreign markets we must accept the most advanced technology available. We must not turn our backs on the difficulties caused by automation. We must face them and enjoy the benefits automation can bring us. In order to do this we must weigh the problems automation is likely to bring before they descend on us, and we have to plan, as we are planning now, for the retraining of those put out of work as a result of automation. Of course, there is little use training people unless we make sure we are training them in an occupation which is likely to be needed. There is little sense training bricklayers to be butchers when what one really needs is electricians. So when we talk about retraining

we must also take steps to ensure we are training people for the right jobs.
I think the difficulties we now encounter have arisen because we did not adapt ourselves quickly enough to new conditions in the changing world around us. I think the formation of an economic council will serve to guard against our making a similar mistake in the future. I think this will be a means by which we can respond to technological changes before, rather than after, they hit us.
I believe the program we are undertaking now is practical and realistic. In these 60 days we are not going to cure all the problems which face us. We are going to begin the cure. During the election campaign we did not promise an instant cure for all the ills which beset the economy. What we did promise was that we would make the decisions necessary to effect a cure. We did promise to introduce realistic programs. We did promise to start on the road to a better future. I believe the measures contained in the speech from the throne indicate we have made that start.

It provides for the greater utilization of existing resources, skills and knowledge, and also provides for the utilization of local councils and for the co-operation of provincial and municipal governments in particular resource areas, primarily rural areas where the problem of hard-core unemployment and seasonal unemployment are most evident. So that this idea that area development policy or an area development agency is new, is a fresh one, or the answer to the problem, is entirely fallacious. These councils, which are already in being or can be brought into being within the scope of the A.R.D.A. program, are today at work and can be further utilized as the people in those various parts of the country who require this kind of assistance get the know-how to utilize available resources.
So, by picking out of the speech at almost any point the allegedly new ideas, we find either things that are not new or things that are simply providing a duplication of services that already exist, and in the case of the Canadian development corporation we might see the creation of a massive corporation. I am told it will be designed to encourage investment by Canadians in their own industries. But it will be a government agency, and it must be remembered there are private agencies capable of doing this. One in particular was created within recent months, the brochure of which was made available to all hon. members of the house. It might even be on their bookshelves right now.

There is one other point on which I certainly do not intend to criticize the government. I only hope it will be able to live up to what it has claimed for itself, and that is its ability to resolve the continuing problem of reaching agreement with the province of British Columbia on the development of the Columbia river. No member of the house could be other than satisfied to learn that the premier of British Columbia is prepared to meet the Prime Minister of Canada in June, to initiate discussions on this question. But may I warn, if it is necessary, the members of the Liberal party and the members of the government that the mere fact the premier of British Columbia is prepared to discuss the subject with them is not necessarily a guarantee that the project will proceed.
By things I heard during the election campaign I am led to believe that the Liberal party wishes to renegotiate certain aspects of the present treaty, and from what we hear from the premier of British Columbia, I am led to believe that he wants certain concessions from the government of Canada.
I have no way of knowing exactly what direction the government's renegotiation commitment will take it, but I am somewhat apprehensive of what the premier of British Columbia will demand in concessions from the federal government. I would like to put three suggestions to the government for consideration on this matter. At this point I do not suggest they are sufficient to provide an entire resolution of the question, because the Columbia river development is complex. Indeed, it is very difficult for a layman to enter into this field without getting himself into trouble. I would suggest to the government however that studies be made of the costs estimates made after the treaty was negotiated, which seem to indicate that the Mica creek dam can be built approximately fifteen feet higher than was originally projected within the costs estimates. If it is possible to increase the height of the Mica creek dam within the present costs estimates, it might provide the opportunity to transfer part of the storage waters of the Arrow lakes to the reservoir behind Mica, and thus eliminate the flooding now contemplated. This in turn would reduce the pressure on the built up areas on the Arrow lakes and also preserve more productive farm land.
I do not know if this is a feasible suggestion, but I do believe its feasibility should be examined in the light of the knowledge that is now available to the government. Perhaps

it could lead the way to the suggestion, made three years ago by General McNaughton, before the external affairs committee of the house when he referred to the possibility of an intermediate Arrow program instead of high Arrow, if low Arrow program was not possible in the complex of over-all development.
I would also like to suggest that the government endeavour to persuade the province of British Columbia that, in a development as large as the Columbia river, the authority which supervises it, whether it be purely provincial or a joint authority shared by both the federal and provincial governments, these should be an over-all authority concerned not just with the building of dams for power generation and the storage of water, but with the redevelopment and relocation of the communities in the whole of the valley, that it provide for the diking and protection of lands where necessary, and that it assist in providing services in those communities to which a large number of workmen and their families will come, such as occurs when a program of this size is undertaken.
If it is true that 3,000 people will be employed for three years at Mica creek, then presumably the city of Revelstoke will have to provide additional water, sewage and other services for a substantial number of people. To the best of my knowledge this problem is not being faced up to by the province of British Columbia at the present time, and the federal government should assure that it be considered.
There is one further step that the federal government might take, and that is to offer the province of British Columbia an outright grant of half the costs of the construction of the transmission lines on the Mica creek project as a first step in the establishment of a national power grid in Canada. I assure the government, interested as this one professes to be in economic development in Canada, that any major step of this kind would lead to tremendous economic growth in British Columbia, and beyond British Columbia in the rest of Canada, if immense resources of electrical power could be moved to other places. In suggesting this I assume the government would be interested in any step that would lead to the establishment of a national power grid system.
In making this suggestion I would point out there are ample precedents for making an outright grant of this kind. These are found in the grants to the maritime provinces, and the grant which forms the federal government's share of the cost of atomic power development in the province of Ontario. This 28902-5-15

We have seen, particularly during the last election campaign, the old parties trying to blame the problems of this country upon the new parties that are growing up in Canada today. They completely ignore the fact that the only reason for the new parties is the failure of the old parties. The problems that we face in this nation today have arisen from a long, long line of small grievances. These grievances have for far too many years been hidden; and hiding solves nothing. Certainly if hiding solved anything, all these problems would have been solved in 96 years. The greatest danger that we face today is that we may go from one extreme to the other.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, allow me to say here that I shudder when I hear irresponsible people speak about the separation of Quebec from the rest of Canada. I was born and educated in Quebec. I served in Quebec regiments, both French and English. As far as I am concerned, Quebec is not only my birthplace, but also the cradle of our nation. Quebec is Canada; how could it be separated from it? (Text):
The thing that raises most fear in my mind, Mr. Speaker, is that the acts of terrorism we see being committed today may prevent a proper solution to these problems which we have had over the years. I should like to make an appeal to both the English and French citizens of our country and ask them to use forbearance at the present time; for the English Canadian to realize that there are grievances which need correction, and for the French Canadian to realize that we will not solve problems in this country of ours by acts of terrorism.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would come to a matter that is of great importance to the constituency which I have the honour to represent. During this session, or certainly during this year, parliament will have to deal with the problem, because it is a measure that is up for consideration. I am referring, of course, to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, which has run its three year course and this year is up for renewal, amendment, or whatever is the will of this parliament. I realize, of course, that we will

The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin have another chance to discuss this matter in possibly more detail when the legislation is before the house. All I wish to do now is impress upon the government the importance of this particular matter.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was first passed by a Liberal government. It has twice been extended by a Conservative government. In fact, the last time it was dealt with the assistance provided under the act was increased by some 25 per cent. Many years have passed since this measure was enacted, and I think we should now realize that in addition to the original purpose of this act-which was of course to foster and maintain the gold mining community-this is a very important matter to our country today. One of the major problems that has plagued this country for a number of years is that we are importing more than we are exporting. Every year this problem is with us. I think we should realize that gold is one product that Canada has in quantity. In fact, Canada is the second highest gold producing country in the world. This is one product that we will never have more of than we can export. We may have a glut of copper, iron, lumber, paper-yes, even of wheat-but gold is one thing we will never have a glut of in this country. Consequently, if we realize the true significance of this product and its value to our country, we should realize that this matter is really the responsibility of the country and the gold mining industry should therefore, in its present circumstances, be subsidized by the country as a whole. It should not be subsidized, as it has been for far too long in the past, by the industry itself, by the people working in that industry and by the merchants and citizens of the communities which are supported by the gold mines. However, I have not changed my opinion that if this act is to serve the purpose for which it was originally passed, some changes must be made to ensure that the benefit of this subsidy paid by the people of Canada shall accrue to the municipalities, to the people working in those municipalities and to those who serve them.
I should like to devote the remainder of my time to a question which I have found to be the number one problem in the riding I represent. There are some who may think that when I deal with this matter I am venturing upon a provincial field, but such is not the case. This subject has a direct interest for the federal government, and more particularly for the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am only sorry that the minister is unable to be here while we are dealing with this matter. I have in mind the great number of cases in my constituency, and, I assume,

The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin in similar constituencies, of people who sustain injuries in the course of their work. Because of the present regulations and practices of the workmen's compensation board of the province of Ontario, these injured workmen become foisted upon the municipal welfare rolls which are supported in their turn by the federal government through the Department of National Health and Welfare.
It is my intention to list just a few of these cases. I can assure hon. members I have hundreds of them on my files. During the last election campaign between 300 and 400 of them came to my attention. I am thinking in particular, now, of a case where a man sustained a broken ankle. After treatment the cast was removed from his ankle and he was instructed by his doctor to take some exercise. While walking across his yard, his ankle buckled under him and he fell, twisting his back, as a result of which he had to spend two or three more weeks in hospital. The compensation board refused to accept that there was any connection between the two accidents. The man's wife and his seven children are now wards of the municipality with 40 per cent of their welfare costs being paid by the federal government.
Many cases arise where there is a delay of six weeks, ten weeks, three months, four months or even five months before a payment is made to these injured workers. Again the situation arises where they must go to the municipality for welfare assistance and where the costs are passed right back to the federal government. I wonder how long we can go on fooling ourselves by believing that we have no real responsibility for what is going on with regard to these particular welfare payments because the money does not appear, in the first instance, to be coming directly from the federal pocket. I think this is a subject which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) and, indeed, the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) might well look into. I can assure them both I can provide hundreds of cases to back up the statements I am making tonight. I sometimes wonder why it is practically impossible to bring this matter adequately to the attention of the public and of those concerned. I have had occasion to write to newspapers, to Toronto daily papers, listing as many as 15 of these cases including the claim numbers, dates and so forth, but not a word will appear in the press. It makes one wonder sometimes if there is not a conspiracy of silence in connection with this matter. I believe the trouble is that the board has been in office far too long. They are looking back with such pride on things they did ten or 15 years ago that they are not even aware of the situation

which prevails today. This is certainly one of the most urgent problems which faces my constituency and I sometimes wonder if a similar situation prevails in all the other constituencies across the province and across Canada.
The whole field of public welfare needs review and revision. I encountered one situation which seems impossible to me in this day and age. It was the case of a man who had an unusually large family, at least for our part of the country. He had some 17 children. Because of the demands of this large family he naturally got behind in paying his bills-an affliction which affects most of us. Of course, the garnishees began to come in and as soon as that happened the man lost his job and had to fall back on municipal welfare relief. Because of the size of his family he was receiving the maximum payment which, in Ontario, is $180 a month. Finally he was able to get a job where he was protected from garnishees. It was a job with the Ontario department of highways. There was one problem, though, he had to take a $20 cut to go to work. His wages came to $160. If he had not gone to work he would have faced a non-support charge and would have gone to jail. 1 think this is a situation which bears looking into. It is an aspect of one of the most pressing problems which faces the new minister as she assumes her duties.
In line with the general trend on this 31st day of decision I think it would be appropriate if I ended my remarks at this point, since we shall have ample time to deal with these matters in the days ahead.

speechtext:
It
is a distinct pleasure for me to begin this, my maiden speech, by offering to you, Mr. Speaker, my congratulations on your election. I know you will fill this high office in a most impressive way and in keeping with the finest of our parliamentary traditions. I am very conscious of the honour which is mine to be speaking in this house for the first time. I feel even more honoured to be speaking as the representative of St. John's East. Historic old St. John's East has now returned happily, and I am confident permanently, to the Liberal vote.
To stand in this parliament of Canada is an experience that for all of us I believe is a memorable one. It is significant in the fact that we are now the chosen representatives not only of the districts from which we come but of the length and breadth of Canada as a whole. I, like many hon. members here, have entered parliament for the first time. They may or may not be awed by the intricacies of constitutional procedure and the varied and complicated order of business; I know

I am. But I know that down deep in our hearts is the dedicated determination to serve worthily and well the people who have sent us here and have entrusted to us their hopes and aspirations. I am very proud to represent St. John's East and I feel that what is good for that district is good for Newfoundland.
Canada's newest province has received some definite and specific undertakings which, when implemented in full, will go far to remove most of the special handicaps under which our province has been operating since confederation. The most forthright of these commitments has been the undertaking of a federal offer of 90 per cent of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway. This, as you know, has been pledged to all the Atlantic provinces, but our province is the only one with a very large unfinished portion of our national highway. Obviously the task is quite beyond the means of our provincial government. It will be remembered, too, that the MacPherson commission strongly recommended its completion at federal cost as a basic national obligation. This, sir, I suggest it is.
Almost above all else Newfoundland vitally needs communications, not only of the physical or material kind-roads such as the Marine drive, with all its maritime magnificence, our long-sought and so badly needed east coast ferry and other ferries and roads- but communications or meetings of minds, so that what is said or sought in Newfoundland is understood and appreciated in Ottawa. This has not always been so in the past.
The 12-mile limit for our hard pressed fishermen is another all important project. Its success, of course, will depend upon the agreement or acquiescence of our American friends. This, I feel, is likely to be forthcoming since the United States associated itself with the six-plus-six resolution which failed by only a very small margin to gain the required two thirds majority at the last law of the sea conference.
The question of fishery development on a national basis is for us of the greatest importance. What will be done in this respect will, of course, depend upon the outcome of a conference which our Prime Minister has offered to call. This will have to be hammered out into a sound economic program that will produce maximum results from efficient direction, financing and supervision.
Newfoundland needs the restoration of the former system of the tax rental agreement. This plan, as you know, Mr. Speaker, made sure that the poorer provinces shared in Canada's growth. Under this system our province will benefit from the expected expansion of our Canadian economy and so would
The Address-Mr. O'Keefe acquire a substantial contribution towards the annual increase in the cost of maintaining our vital public services. What is of crucial, over-riding importance, however, is that our new national policy will consider all these things and others in terms of what is required to overcome inherent disabilities in all the provinces.
I will not dwell at any great length on all, or even many, of the needs of Newfoundland. Some good was done for St. John's East and other districts and provinces by the previous government. After all, they held power for nearly six years, so they could scarcely help doing some good. Yet a great deal more needs to be done now. From time to time I am quite sure that Newfoundland's representatives, all seven of us-all we had to offer- will be heard on behalf of the oldest part of this new country.
Mr. Speaker, the prevailing standards of living in Newfoundland, it seems to me, are maintained to a very large degree by the expenditure of either the federal or provincial governments on various public services, social security and welfare. In places such as Bell island, with its labour surplus, the standard of living is still lower. Of all of this great district, I am painfully anxious that something be done for so long neglected Bell island.
I should like to devote the remainder of my speech to telling you and the house of my native province of Newfoundland and of its natural grandeur, just as others have done with their provinces. However, my people have sent me here to represent them and to act as their spokesman. This is my duty and this I am determined to do as best I can. For this reason I am going to take the few minutes at my disposal to lay before you some details of a situation about which I feel very strongly both the house and the nation should be informed and about which I can no longer remain silent.
Mr. Speaker, my district includes the large island in Conception bay that we call Bell island, with its large town of Wabana, a beautiful Beothic Indian name meaning "land of the rising sun". Some 14,000 people make their homes on this island. I only wish I could tell you that they also make their living there, but that is not so. These 14,000 people do not make a living on Bell island. These men and women, all of them fine Newfoundlanders and Canadians, are doomed by forces seemingly beyond their control to live in circumstances which in case after case approach utter destitution. Do not misunderstand me, sir. I am not saying that each and every one of these fine souls is unable to earn his or her daily bread, for that is not so. But what is true, and tragically true, is that of these 14,000 the staggering number of
